en: The Mahāsannipāta-sūtra-rāja, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Furthermore, while this Dharma was being taught, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat. One...
Having adjusted his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) over one shoulder, he knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
I wish to ask a few questions; may the Buddha grant me permission. Please provide an explanation for whatever I ask."
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra,
ask the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha whatever you desire.”
"Regarding that which you ask, I shall explain it for you so as to bring joy to your heart.
When he had spoken thus, the Venerable Śāriputra said,
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"
"If it should rain upon this Jambudvīpa, where must it rain for it to be called 'good rain'?
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, Śāriputra!"

With your sublime eloquence, you have well contemplated such meanings and wish to question the Tathāgata. You do so for the sake of benefiting many sentient beings, for the sake of enabling many people to attain peace and happiness, out of compassion for the world and for the benefit, peace, and happiness of devas and humans, and also for the sake of inspiring the power of diligence in all sons and daughters of good family who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle in the present and the future.
Śāriputra! Listen well and reflect well!
I shall speak for you.
Śāriputra said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I now delight to hear it."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: “Śāriputra!

Whatever sugarcane, grapes, barley, wheat, sesame, rice, millet, small beans, large beans, mung beans, kidney beans, *kaṭuka-haridrā* beans—which resemble large beans—there may be among the people of Jambudvīpa, these do not exist there. For such fields and other crops as these, rain falling upon that place is called ‘virtuous rain.’”
Why is this? Because if various flavors are produced there, the people of Jambudvīpa are able to use them to sustain their lives; therefore, the rain that falls there is called "excellent rain."
Śāriputra spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
If sons of good family or daughters of good family wish to give the gift of Dharma, in what manner must they give it for it to be called a ‘virtuous gift’?”
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!
When I speak of the gift of Dharma, if one bestows the universal Dharma everywhere, it is called ‘giving well.’”
Śāriputra! I shall now speak further:
when one gives the gift of Dharma to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, this is called the supreme and excellent giving within the gift of Dharma.

Why is this? Because that son of good family seeks the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; therefore, when he bestows that Dharma upon them, it is called the supreme and excellent gift. Śāriputra!
For example, Śāriputra, just as rain falling upon the great ocean does not fail to have fruit and is not without utility,
so too, Śāriputra,
when one gives the gift of Dharma to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, it does not fail to have fruit and is not without utility.
Why is this? Because that son of good family seeks the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, Śāriputra!
For example, Śāriputra, when someone polishes and cleanses a maṇi jewel, if they apply diligent effort, it is called "skillful action.
Why is that? Śāriputra!
When polishing a mani-jewel, one provides it with hundreds of thousands of crystal beads and the like.
In this way, Śāriputra,
if one exerts effort toward bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, it is called "doing good."
Why is this? Because that son of good family, for the sake of all sentient beings, shall seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and set forth in the practice of unsurpassed bodhi.
Śāriputra! It is, for example, like the great ocean, which has no place where it cannot descend and no place where it cannot enter. Why is this?
The great ocean gradually deepens and the great ocean gradually descends; therefore, there is no place where it cannot descend and no place where it cannot enter.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path through skillful means within the perfection of wisdom, there is no dharma that they cannot explain. Śāriputra!

For example, suppose a single drop of water in a pond gives rise to the leaves of an utpala lotus. Although they are from the same pond, the outer leaves of that flower are not so wondrous; they do not receive such praise or esteem, whereas the inner flower is praised and esteemed by both men and women.
In this way, Śāriputra!

Although the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have realized the same single dharma-realm, they do not receive such praise and esteem; however, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is praised and esteemed by the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
Therefore, Śāriputra!
Seeing this meaning, sons of good family and daughters of good family should give rise to this thought:

"Let us not attain the realization of the single dharma-realm and receive the names of śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, nor obtain such praise and honor as those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas do. We should now resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so that we may obtain such praise and honor as those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
"Śāriputra! It is, for example, as with a *śrīkhaṇḍa* tree or a sandalwood tree: its leaves cannot be praised or esteemed as highly as the fragrance of their own substance."
In this way, Śāriputra!

Having realized the same single dharma-realm, the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas does not attain fullness like the fragrance of reality; however, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is fully endowed with the true fragrance.
Śāriputra!
Seeing this meaning, all roots of goodness possessed by sons of good family and daughters of good family should be dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Śāriputra! I say that those who, being fulfilled by spiritual friends, take delight and find joy in unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I instruct them to practice diligently so that they may continue to find such delight and joy.”
Why is this? Śāriputra!
It was because I was formerly sustained by spiritual friends that I have now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Śāriputra! Suppose there is one person who wishes to take precious jewels, and a second person likewise wishes to take jewels; if that first person shows the second person the path toward the jewel island and the place where the jewels are found, I say that this person has no stinginess.
In this way, Śāriputra!
If one shows the path to the jewel-island of omniscience, I say that such a person is likewise free from stinginess. Śāriputra!

It is like a precious gem of great value, worth many hundreds of thousands, which emerges from the great ocean; while the gem is still in the sea, no one polishes it, but once it reaches Jambudvīpa, it is then polished.

Thus it is, Śāriputra! If there are those who wish to see the Tathāgata, they shall resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having each beheld the supreme merits of the Buddha, they will first extensively practice and become *śrāvakas*; having practiced extensively, they will become *pratyekabuddhas*; and having practiced extensively, they will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. All other roots of goodness, through encountering virtuous friends, will likewise become vast and great.

Śāriputra! Seeing this meaning, sons of good family and daughters of good family should seek out virtuous friends, draw near to them, and serve them; having served them, they must cultivate many practices, and before long they will attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because in the past, I too was sustained by spiritual friends, and thus have now attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Śāriputra!..."

It is like a mani jewel: when it is being polished, fine dust falls away; yet that fine dust cannot be praised or valued in the same way as that great mani jewel, which is praised and valued by kings, royal ministers, and other wise people who are able to distinguish jewels.
In this way, Śāriputra!

Although the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have realized the same single dharma-realm, they do not receive such praise and esteem; however, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is praised and esteemed by the world’s gods, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth.
Śāriputra! It is as if, for example, someone were to take a lump of gold and go to a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice, and having arrived, say to them:
"Take this gold and fashion it into an anklet for me; I shall wear it on my foot."
Then that goldsmith, or his apprentice, said to the man:

"I shall fashion a necklace from this gold for you to wear upon your head, neck, or hand; once it is fastened, many hundreds of thousands of people will see it and feel great joy, and they will praise you."
"Śāriputra! At that time, that foolish man did not accept the beneficial and kind words of the goldsmith, but replied to him, saying:
'You need only make an anklet for me.'"
"Thus it is, Śāriputra!

When a son of good family or a daughter of good family is performing a supreme act of giving in the presence of the Tathāgata or in the presence of a śrāvaka, if some spiritual friend should come to them and say:
'O Noble One!'"
That you now perform this supreme act of giving, yet do not accord with what is wholesome— namely,
that by means of this supreme act of giving, you dedicate the merit toward the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha within the sphere of conditioned phenomena— is not right.
"By performing this supreme dharma of giving, all the roots of goodness therein are capable of being dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Śāriputra!
Among all mundane and supramundane dharmas, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the most supreme and skillful wisdom.
Śāriputra, for this reason,
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, praise anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because this is the unsurpassed dedication, namely, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Śāriputra!
Seeing this meaning, sons of good family and daughters of good family should dedicate all their roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Śāriputra! Suppose there are two men, one of whom is skilled at weaving golden *karpāsa* fibers produced from the same tree, crafting fine garments worth hundreds of thousands.”
A certain man, wishing to have a coarse garment made for a servant, went to a weaver and said:
"Good sir! I have this golden *karpāsa* thread, well-prepared and all from the same tree; weave it well for me."
The weaver replied, "O noble sir!
I shall provide you with a garment worth a hundred thousand; what need have you for a coarse cloth?"
That man did not accept the weaver’s kind words, but replied to the weaver, saying:
"Simply make for me a coarse garment suitable for a servant.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Although they share the same Dharma and the same roots of goodness, some may take the stage of the śrāvaka as their object of focus, some may take the stage of the pratyekabuddha as their object of focus, and some may abide in the unsurpassed path.
Śāriputra! If among them there should be anyone who takes as an object of focus the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, you should say to them:
"These roots of goodness of yours are the causes for the Tathāgata."
If there is one who seeks unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi, they should also say:
"All the roots of goodness from this Dharma-giving of yours should be gathered into a single mass and dedicated toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Dedicating in this manner, one should give those roots of goodness to all sentient beings and embrace them with an inexhaustible mind. By virtue of these roots of goodness, one should wish that all sentient beings may attain the fulfillment of inconceivable wisdom, incomparable wisdom, and the supreme, unsurpassed wisdom of the three realms, just like that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Śāriputra! Seeing this meaning, sons of good family and daughters of good family should plant roots of goodness for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Śāriputra! It is like a king whose chief queen gives birth to eight sons.

Among all these sons, there is only one who possesses the marks of a king; he succeeds to the royal throne and receives the consecration with water, while the remaining princes all surround him and serve him according to the law.”
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Is it not the fault of that mother’s womb that prevented the other princes from being consecrated to the position of great king?
Śāriputra said: "No,
Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"

Why is this? Because those other princes did not perform royal duties in the past nor plant roots of goodness; for these reasons, none of those other princes were able to succeed to the consecrated royal throne.
The Buddha said: "So it is,
Śāriputra!"

Once they have equally realized the single Dharma-realm, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas receive the title of "Dharma Kings," while the other sons of good family receive the name of "Śrāvakas. Is it not the case that there is some fault in this Dharma-realm?
Śāriputra said:
"No, World-Honored One."

It is not that this dharma-realm has any fault; rather, it is because those individuals in former times were unable to dedicate their roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment, did not practice this path, made no aspirational vows, failed to cultivate superior roots of goodness, and did not seek the benefit of omniscience—that they now give rise only to the state of a śrāvaka.

They do not practice the conduct of a Tathāgata, nor do they possess the qualities of a Tathāgata; they lack the supernormal powers (abhijñā) such as those of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
“Śāriputra! For this reason, sons of good family and daughters of good family should dedicate all the roots of goodness they have cultivated toward unsurpassed bodhi.”
Śāriputra! It is like the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees; when they first sprout, all the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rejoice greatly and say:
"Now that these trees have grown in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it shall not remain empty for long."
"Thus it is, Śāriputra!

There may be times when sons of good family or daughters of good family resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta. At that time, all those who have right faith in the Triple Gem—the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—will feel joy and exultation, thinking: 'This site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) should not remain empty for long; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva shall attain unexcelled bodhi.'"

“Śāriputra! For example, when the Trāyastriṃśa gods see the leaves emerging from the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees, they do not praise or honor them; however, when they see the flowers, their hearts are filled with joy and exultation.”
In this way, Śāriputra!

Although the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas realize the single dharma-realm, the gods and people of the world do not praise or honor them; yet, if they see a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, their hearts leap with joy.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is endowed with all roots of goodness and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; his radiance surpasses that of the sun and moon, and he is able to illuminate immeasurable Buddha-fields out of compassion for sentient beings.

“Śāriputra! For example, when that pārijātaka-kovidāra tree is growing, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven should know that before long this tree will have many leaves—hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of leaves, even up to immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas of leaves—to cover its top.”
In this way, Śāriputra!

You should know that when those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have first resolved upon awakening are born, for a long duration there will be hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of śrāvakas, even up to immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya assemblies of śrāvakas surrounding them in front, and many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas will appear.
Śāriputra!

For example, on Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, there are distinct peaks that are one hundred yojanas high, or two hundred yojanas high, up to seven hundred yojanas high; these distinct peaks cannot be called the Great Mount Sumeru.
In this way, Śāriputra!

Although śrāvakas are born from the wisdom of the Tathāgata, one cannot say that their wisdom is as complete as that of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; nor do they possess the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the wisdom of the four fearlessnesses, the unimpeded wisdom, and so forth.
However, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do indeed possess all the powers, fearlessnesses, unimpeded wisdoms, and the like.

Śāriputra! Just as it should be known that at the abode of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there dwell many hosts of devaputras—hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas, even up to immeasurable and boundless hosts of devaputras—who appear upon its summit; there they enjoy celestial rewards with great delight, and whenever they wish to roam through the celestial realms, they do so at will.
In this way, Śāriputra!

When those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have first resolved their minds for awakening give rise to long-enduring roots of goodness dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment, you should know that there will appear in the world many assemblies of śrāvakas—hundreds of thousands, koṭis, nayutas, and even immeasurable and boundless numbers of śrāvakas—who shall roam at will through all the abodes of the noble ones.
“Śāriputra! For example, the abode of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, has four sides that exist simultaneously, with no sequence of before or after.
In the same way, Śāriputra!”

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dedicates their roots of goodness toward unexcelled enlightenment, at that very moment, buddha-nature, the stage of a buddha, buddha-wisdom, and the virtues of a buddha are all produced simultaneously, without any sequence of before or after.
Śāriputra! For example, even if the abode of Sumeru, the king of mountains, were broken into pieces, it would still be higher and greater than other mountains.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

When that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment dedicates their roots of goodness toward unsurpassed bodhi, even compared to all other roots of goodness, this alone is sufficient to serve as the most supreme, lofty, and stable foundation.

Śāriputra! It is as if Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, has golden slopes; if any birds or beasts reach those slopes, they all become one color—namely, gold—and thus share the same color as the lion, the king of beasts.

Śāriputra! Although they may share the same golden color as the lion, king of beasts, their power, majesty, merit, and renown are in no way equal to those of the lion king; furthermore, they do not possess the lion king’s playful stretching, his fearlessness, or his roaring voice.
In this way, Śāriputra!

Although the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas share the same single flavor as the Tathāgata—namely, the flavor of liberation—they cannot be equal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. They do not possess such qualities of the Tathāgata as the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), or the lion’s roar.
However, the Tathāgata is endowed with the various dharmas of skillful means and wisdom; these skillful means and wisdom are not even heard of by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone produced.
The merit of the Tathāgata, the play of the Tathāgata, and the thunderous voice of the Tathāgata—the Tathāgata roars with the lion’s roar, rising high above all worlds. Śāriputra!
Just as various birds and beasts may share the same color as the lion king, yet because their other qualities are not equal to his, they cannot be called "lion kings of beasts."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Although the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas share the same taste of liberation as the Tathāgata, they are nonetheless not equal to the Tathāgata. This is because they do not attain the merit or the renown [of a Buddha], nor do they attain the supreme-of-the-supreme name of the Tathāgata or the essence of the Tathāgata;

furthermore, they do not attain unsurpassed enlightenment, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unimpeded wisdoms, and so forth. Because he is fully endowed with these powers, fearlessnesses, and unimpeded wisdoms, he is called the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Śāriputra! Because of seeing this meaning, whatever roots of goodness are performed by sons of good family or daughters of good family, all should be dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi. "Śāriputra!"
For example, the gods of the Four Great Kings dwell all around the slopes of Mount Sumeru, while the Trāyastriṃśa gods dwell upon its summit.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
“Does Mount Sumeru not accommodate the gods of the Four Great Kings?
Yet, do those Four Kings not dwell upon its summit?
Śāriputra replied, “No.”
World-Honored One!

It is not that Mount Sumeru cannot accommodate the gods of the Four Great Kings, yet they do not dwell there; it is simply because in the past they did not plant the seeds of merit for enjoyment upon the mountain. Since they did not perform such karma, they are unable to dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
“In this way, Śāriputra!

This Dharma-body of mine is likewise without fault, yet it does not accommodate those such as the śrāvakas, causing them to fail to attain the wisdom of the worlds of the ten directions. Because in the past they did not know how to dedicate their roots of goodness toward unsurpassed bodhi, nor did they make vows to cultivate such practices, nor did they give rise to the mind of supreme, universal knowledge; for this reason, they have now become śrāvakas, unable to roam within the sphere of the Tathāgata’s activity, lacking the merits of a Tathāgata, and not being endowed with the powers, fearlessnesses, or unimpeded wisdoms.
Because the Buddha is fully endowed with these wisdoms, he is named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Śāriputra! Just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse,
so it is, Śāriputra!
An avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell together with stinginess.
Śāriputra! It is, for example, like the tide of the great ocean, which never fails its appointed time.
In this way, Śāriputra,
when a mendicant comes to an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva, he never fails to arrive at the appointed time. Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, it is just as if someone were to take a drop of water from the great ocean; all would be of one taste, namely, the taste of salt.

In the same way, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates various roots of goodness performed through hundreds of thousands of different gateways toward unexcelled enlightenment, they all become of one taste, namely, the taste of omniscience.
Śāriputra!

It is like the nature of gold that produces gold—that is, gold ore—which, according to various intentions, is fashioned into various ornaments and thereby receives the various names of those ornaments.
In this way, Śāriputra!
A single Buddha-wisdom is transformed into many hundreds of thousands of various necklaces, namely, the production of the roots of goodness in sentient beings. Śāriputra!

Just as when a king mints coins, those that have already been stamped with an inscription are called "coins," whereas those not yet stamped and lacking an inscription do not receive the name of "coin.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have not yet bestowed upon them the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Once they have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, then bestow the prediction, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
"In a future age, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Śāriputra, it is like an outsider seer who possesses the divine eye;

if he sees someone newly dwelling within the womb, whose physical characteristics have not yet been determined because the marks of male or female have not yet formed, then at a later time, once the marks of male or female have formed, the outsider seer will finally use his divine eye to predict, saying, "This one shall be born as a male" or "This one shall be born as a female."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

As long as a bodhisattva has not yet attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have not yet bestowed upon them the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
If they subsequently attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will then bestow upon them this prediction:
"O son of good family!
In a future age, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Śāriputra! For example, when the orb of the sun rises, it does not form this thought:
'My light shall illuminate this Jambudvīpa.'"
"However, whenever the sun emerges together with its light, it will surely provide illumination for Jambudvīpa, making all the various forms of the people in Jambudvīpa clearly manifest."
In this way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the wisdom of omniscience, he does not form the thought:
"I shall illuminate the trichiliocosm."

"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this dharma-conduct, sits upon this ground, possesses these marks of birth, and possesses these roots of goodness, he shall awaken to wisdom in such a manner."
By means of this awakened wisdom, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will surely illuminate the trichiliocosm for himself.
Śāriputra, it is like two people who both wish to obtain treasures and enter a treasure island; there, one person takes a priceless jewel, while the second person takes a jewel of value.
Then the wise man said: "O noble sir!
There is a priceless jewel here; you may take it."
This jewel is of great value; kings, ministers, city-dwellers, and other wise people who possess specialized knowledge of gems all together praise it as being precious and supreme.
"Because this person did not heed that other person's words, he took the priceless jewel.
In the same way, Śāriputra, this Buddha-dharma is also like a jewel island;

once someone has arrived there, they immediately form the thought of it being priceless and practice its full perfection—namely, the mindfulness associated with the jewel of omniscient wisdom, which is far removed from the thoughts of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Furthermore, there is a second person who practices mindfulness associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Śāriputra!
Having realized the same single Dharma-realm, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is reckoned among the ranks of the Dharma Kings.
Furthermore, there are other sons of good family who, having become śrāvakas, are numbered among the śrāvakas;
those who have attained omniscience are numbered among the universal seers, such as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
“Śāriputra! It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel: whosoever holds it in their hand gains mastery over it, and there is no treasure they cannot obtain.”

Thus, Śāriputra, there is not a single being for whom a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perform the work of a jewel; there is not a single being for whom they do not teach the cultivation of roots of goodness, up to and including unconditioned nirvāṇa.

Śāriputra! It is like a person who carves a maṇi jewel, or a disciple of such a person: whatever impurities or defects exist on the surface of the gem, once it has been polished and rubbed, its brilliance and color become supreme.
Once they have recognized the excellence of the gem, those jewel-makers or their disciples shall acquire many hundreds of thousands of accumulations of wealth by which they sustain their lives.
In this same way, Śāriputra!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva causes roots of goodness to arise in others according to their individual minds; he then gathers all those roots of goodness through the skillful wisdom of his own mind, and by means of these roots of goodness, he accomplishes all Buddha-dharmas.
Śāriputra! Just as a maṇi jewel, when it has not yet been purified, must be carefully concealed. Why is this?
Because that mani-jewel is priceless.
In this same way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolves upon the mind of awakening, he should be protected by the devas, humans, gandharvas, and asuras of the world.
Why is this? Because that virtuous man has resolved his mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras.
Śāriputra!

Just as a mani-jewel, even before it has been polished, should be known as something praised and held in high esteem by kings, ministers, city-dwellers, and other wise people who possess the specialized knowledge of gems.

In this way, Śāriputra, you should know that those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have first resolved their minds [toward awakening] are likewise praised and held in high esteem by the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as well as by bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Śāriputra! For example, when someone sees a Buddha, they should give rise to a sense of rare wonder, thinking: "A Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world only from time to time.

I should now resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and cultivate the karma of the true Dharma. By means of this teaching of the true Dharma, I shall cause all sentient beings to gather roots of goodness, and all those roots of goodness shall be dedicated toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

When he is dedicating [merit], if there should be monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who lack faith, or if Māraputrās or Mārakāyika devas come to his place and speak of the faults of the Mahāyāna, causing him to abandon it and lose his aspiration for it.
Śāriputra, what do you think? Would they not indeed bring about harm,
lack of benefit, lack of peace, suffering, and downfall for many hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of sentient beings, even unto immeasurable, boundless, and asaṃkhyeya sentient beings?
Śāriputra said: “It is so, Blessed One.”
So it is, Great Virtuous Sugata! Why is that?

They act to the detriment and for the lack of peace of all sentient beings, causing them suffering and causing them to fall; that is to say, they speak of faults regarding the Mahāyāna to sons of good family and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna, causing them to take no delight in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, causing them to retreat, and causing them to depart from it.
The Buddha said: “Śāriputra!
If you wish not to abandon the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, you should seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Therefore, Śāriputra, all sons and daughters of good family who have set out upon the Great Vehicle should aspire to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they must neither regress nor turn away from it.

Why is this? When I speak of not abandoning the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, I refer to sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna and who, regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, desire it with joy, remaining neither separated from it nor regressing.
Śāriputra! It is like this:
for example, in an age of famine and calamity, what is sown does not grow, as if one were sowing upon a stone.

At that time, whether it be a king or a royal minister, a kṣatriya or a kṣatriya minister, a brāhmaṇa or a great brāhmaṇa family, a householder or a householder’s wife, or a great householder family—these, for the sake of the multitude in the cities and towns, gather various kinds of grain and construct great granaries.
At that time, the multitude all went to the granary, took various kinds of grain, and returned home to eat it.
Then, one person arrived at the site of the granary and set fire to it, burning it down.
Śāriputra, what do you think? Would such unwholesome persons not cause harm,

bring about lack of peace and security, and lead to suffering and downfall for many hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas, even up to immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings?
"These are what are called unwholesome people; they set fire to that granary and burn it to ruin, so that no one may enjoy its use.
Śāriputra said, "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

In this way, when the True Dharma is about to perish, there may be someone who hears that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared in the world at some time; having heard this, they give rise to great compassion toward sentient beings, and having given rise to great compassion, they resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, if there should arise unwholesome persons who speak of faults regarding the Mahāyāna to sons of good family and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna, causing them to lack aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, causing them to retreat, and causing them to depart from it.
Śāriputra, what do you think? This unwholesome person brings about harm and lack of peace for immeasurable,

boundless, asaṃkhyeya sentient beings, causing them suffering and causing them to fall— namely, by speaking of faults regarding the Mahāyāna to sons of good family and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna, thereby causing them to lose their aspiration for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, causing them to retreat, and causing them to depart from it.
Śāriputra said: “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
“Śāriputra! It is as if a caravan leader were leading many merchants along a road when they encountered a great, perilous river with abundant flowing water.
At that time, one man spoke thus to a second man:”
"O man! You should employ skillful means, devise a plan, and exert your strength to seek out a boat.
Then the second person said to that man:
"I am currently staying here and cannot find a boat.

At that time, that person was resolute and capable, diligently employing skillful means to seek out a boat and bring it to the riverbank; thus, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings were able to cross from this shore to the other shore, and having crossed, they dwelt upon that shore.
The second person, however, was indolent, ignorant, weak, and of meager merit; he remained at his original location and was unable to cross the river.

Furthermore, there were other people who came to the riverbank also wishing to cross; seeing that person who was indolent, lacking wisdom, weak in strength, and of meager merit, they said to him: "O man!..."
"Why do you not ferry them across?
At that time, the lazy person spoke these words:

"My companions used skillful means and exerted effort to obtain a boat and place it by the riverbank; they have already enabled hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of sentient beings to cross from this shore to the other shore."
Then those other people said to that person:
"O you who are so lazy and indolent, why did you not follow your companions, but instead fall into this place to undergo immeasurable suffering?"
"Thus it is, Śāriputra!
I see two people practicing generosity, and one says to the second person:
'O worthy man!'"
"You should apply yourself appropriately, employ skillful means and exert effort, and gather roots of goodness for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The second person said, "I do not take up *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; I only wish to reach the stage of an arhat."

If one wishes to reach the state of an Arhat, one must likewise employ appropriate skillful means and exert effort; one shall then attain birth in the first dhyāna, and likewise attain birth in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception. Should one pass away during that interval, by virtue of this one will be reborn in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, where the body shall obtain long life and dwell for a duration of eighty-four thousand kalpas.

At that time, that person realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Having awakened, he taught the Dharma for the sake of many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of sentient beings, even unto immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Having taught the Dharma, he subsequently entered parinirvāṇa through the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
"At that time, the second person, riding upon this, remains dwelling in that Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
When he had spoken thus, the Venerable Śāriputra said, "So it is."
"O Bhagavān, it is so! O Sugata, it is so!"
"It is indeed as the Tathāgata has said, World-Honored One!

You should know that such a person is indolent. If one delights in the first dhyāna up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, and becomes attached to those realms, then having become so attached, one can no longer harmonize with the qualities of superior persons; one does not apply skillful means or exert effort, does not draw near to, follow, or serve virtuous friends, and does not contemplate the three gates of liberation as they truly are. You should know that this is an indolent person."
“World-Honored One!
That bodhisattva-mahāsattva exerts great diligence, whereas the śrāvaka’s meager faith is his indolence.
World-Honored One!”
Seeing this meaning, sons of good family and daughters of good family should dedicate all their roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Śāriputra! It is like a maṇi jewel that possesses manifold functions; suppose one were to ask the person who fashioned the maṇi jewel, ‘What functions does this maṇi jewel have?’”
Having been thus questioned, he explained it according to what he knew; therein, if one knew much, he spoke much, and if one knew little, he spoke little.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Once they have equally realized the single Dharma-realm, there are those who are reborn as wise Śrāvakas; they know according to their superior qualities and speak according to their superior qualities, answering questions in accordance with what was asked, based on limited knowledge because of their former limited vows.

However, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses infinite wisdom; because he made infinite vows in the past, he possesses infinite, unimpeded wisdom and infinite perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), through skillful means bringing sentient beings to maturity.

Why is this? Because when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he accumulated boundless vows; by means of these adornments of boundless meritorious dharmas, he realized universal wisdom (sarvajñatā).

Śāriputra! For example, when the *pārijātaka* and *kovidāra* trees first produce their small blossoms, they emit a fragrance that surpasses all other flowers grown in this Jambudvīpa—whether they be *sumana*, *bharīśa*, or *campaka*, or any other flowers that may grow there—for none of those can equal the fragrance of the small blossoms first produced by the *pārijātaka* and *kovidāra* trees.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Whatever roots of goodness possessed by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—whether their renown, fragrance, majestic power, or strength—none can equal that of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening (*bodhicitta*). How much less so those who have entered the practice, how much less so those who are non-regressive, how much less so those in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), how much less so those who have reached the time of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), how much less so those who abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, how much less so those at the supreme site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and how much less so the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; for they possess all fragrance, all majestic power, and all strength, being fully endowed with such power as the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Śāriputra! For example, all the springs, bathing pools, lakes, ponds, small rivers, and great rivers that exist in this Jambudvīpa flow into the great ocean, yet the great ocean is never satiated.

In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is never satiated with the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā); likewise, they are never satiated with the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), skillful means (upāya), and omniscience (sarvajñatā), nor with any of their roots of goodness (kuśalamūla).
Śāriputra! For example, all the flowing springs, bathing pools, lakes, small rivers, and great rivers that exist within this Jambudvīpa are entirely contained and received within the great ocean.
In this way, Śāriputra!

All devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and indeed all realms of sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to contain and sustain them all, bestowing upon them the flavor of ambrosia to bring them joy.
“Śāriputra! For example,
just as the armor worn by the great nāga, the powerful mahāpuruṣa deity, cannot be worn by any person of Jambudvīpa,
so it is, Śāriputra!”
The armor donned by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within the Buddha-dharma is the very armor they don for the sake of all sentient beings; that armor cannot be donned by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
In this way, Śāriputra!

From the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting at the supreme site of enlightenment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon such armor and practices the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Śāriputra! Sons and daughters of good family who have first resolved upon the Great Vehicle should train in this manner, applying themselves with diligence and exerting effort in their practice; thus they shall swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Śāriputra! Just as all the trees on the southern slopes of the King of Snow Mountains possess various flowers, fruits, and fragrances, yet the people of Jambudvīpa are unable to make use of them; so it is with these trees.
In this way, Śāriputra!

Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess the roots of goodness consisting of untainted morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, sentient beings cannot make use of them.

Just as the roots of goodness consisting of the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall be utilized by all sentient beings.

Śāriputra! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should don such armor: that all sentient beings may make use of whatever roots of goodness there are—namely, morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

"If sentient beings were unable to make use of them, I would not possess such roots of goodness—namely, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Śāriputra! [he said.]

For example, when the great river Gaṅgā flows, the place where it flows moistens this great earth, making it lush and fertile; furthermore, as that flow moves along, pressing against the ground, it sweeps away all dust, soil, grass, trees, leaves, and the like.
In this way, Śāriputra,

wherever a bodhisattva mahāsattva walks, stands, sits, or lies down within Jambudvīpa— in such places as these— he gathers in all sentient beings, causing their roots of goodness to become moistened and nourished.

Furthermore, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he performs these acts while fully embracing all oppressive unwise conducts, as well as the conducts of desire, hatred, and delusion, and all inverted behaviors.
Śāriputra! If sons or daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna hear what has been said above, even if they are greatly indolent, they must nonetheless exert great diligence.
Śāriputra! For example, as the great river Gaṅgā flows, in some places it makes a loud sound, in some places it makes little sound, and in some places it is silent.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) manifest the production of roots of goodness in some places; in other places, they manifest themselves as attending upon and serving spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); and in yet other places, they manifest themselves as acting as spiritual friends for others. In accordance with what the vessels of sentient beings can endure, they manifest themselves in such ways.
Śāriputra! For example, if a mirror-disk has not been well-polished and is not clear, the reflection seen within it will likewise not be clear;
only when that mirror-disk has been well-polished and made clean will its reflection be seen with distinct clarity.
Thus, Śāriputra!

A beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon seeing his own roots of goodness, should attend upon a spiritual friend; by attending upon a spiritual friend, he subsequently causes the Buddha-dharma to increase.

“Śāriputra! For example, when the great river Gaṅgā is swelling and full, all the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves upon its two banks are carried away by the current, even unto the four great oceans.”
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should don such armor:
"Whatever dark deeds on this shore lead to falling away, or whatever perilous paths of various views I may travel, I shall carry them all away until I reach the realm of nirvana without remainder."

Śāriputra! It is as if, for instance, at times the great river Gaṅgā swells with much foam, and within it there are many trees and such, whose roots, trunks, leaves, and fruits have been uprooted and carried away; yet among them, there remains another great tree that continues to grow and stand.
Later, in the second year, the great river Gaṅgā became even longer than before, and the great trees previously there, along with all the other timber, were uprooted and carried away.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having served virtuous friends and resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nevertheless follow along with the enjoyment of the five desires and the experience of pleasure due to the power of evil friends and the force of their past karmic actions, they must subsequently serve virtuous friends once more until they attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Why is this? Because the roots of goodness planted in the presence of the Buddhas shall never be in vain; they will certainly appear in the world as Buddhas, known by the name "Omniscient One" (Samantabhadra) and the name "Universal Seer" (Samantadarśin).

“Śāriputra! It is as if at some time there were a conflagration at the end of an eon; at that time, this trichiliocosm would all be intensely ablaze, emitting light of a single uniform incandescence, such that whether burning or being destroyed, it would be without soot and without shadow.”
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should don such armor:

"Not a single sentient being is to be perceived; among all those in the realm of sentient beings, there are none who do not know [this]. For them, I shall cause them to attain the dharma of non-retrogression."
Śāriputra! For example, when that great mass of flames burns, all poisons and medicinal herbs are equally consumed by the fire.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should don such armor as this: whether there are sentient beings who have a vehicle or sentient beings who do not have a vehicle, I shall preach the Dharma equally to them all; according to their aspirations and according to their faiths, I shall swiftly enable those various sentient beings of diverse faiths and practices to cross over, without forming dualistic conceptions.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are non-dual and do not manifest as dual characteristics; all phenomena are selfless, and within suchness, there is no knowing.
"Śāriputra!..."
Śāriputra, it is just as when a great mass of flames burns, although there are flames even reaching up to the Ābhāsvara Heaven, they cannot reach such a vast distance.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

Having realized the same dharmadhātu, although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas enter it equally, their wisdom does not function throughout the worlds of the ten directions, unlike those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who, having realized the dharmadhātu, possess immeasurable wisdom.
Śāriputra! For example, that great mass of fire neither comes from nor goes to the worlds of the ten directions, yet it burns the trichiliocosm; furthermore, that fire is not without a cause.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

That wisdom of the Buddhas does not come from, nor go to, the worlds of the ten directions, nor do they gather together therein. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is endowed with perfect wisdom, knows the mental activities of all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions as they truly are; that wisdom is likewise not without cause. Such is how the supreme, universal wisdom should be viewed.
“Śāriputra! For example, when the orb of the sun rises, you should know that it eclipses all fireflies and brings forth its illumination.
In the same way, Śāriputra!”

When a bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment, for as long as they live, one should know that they outshine the light of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who possess the wisdom of the various perfections, and act as a radiance. Why is this?
He dedicates the roots of goodness he has cultivated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; for this reason, he possesses boundless light. Śāriputra!
For example, when the solar orb rises, you should know that it eclipses the colors and lights of all the stars and shines forth its radiance, so that the starlight in all places is no longer seen.

In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva descends from the Tuṣita heaven, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of devas come to Jambudvīpa and utter such sounds, proclaim such sounds, and speak such words:
"O you people! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is now casting off his body from the Tuṣita celestial palace."
At that time, all the pratyekabuddhas in this Jambudvīpa who possessed great wisdom, having heard this sound, resolved their minds toward nirvana. Why was this?

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Supreme Field of Merit, descended from Tuṣita Heaven, he possessed such sovereign power; how much more so when he was born, when he took seven steps, and when he first uttered the words: "I am the greatest and most supreme in the world; I shall surely bring an end to birth, old age, sickness, and death. How much more so when he departed [from the palace], when he reached the site of enlightenment, and when he realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, among all sentient beings, the Tathāgata may be called the most supreme, the most exalted, the greatest, the most wondrous, the unsurpassed, and the unsurpassably unsurpassed.
Śāriputra!
Seeing this meaning, sons of good family and daughters of good family should dedicate all the roots of goodness they have performed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Śāriputra! For example, all the seeds that exist upon the great earth produce sprouts that have various names; yet they share the same earthly dust and possess their respective characteristics.”
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Having realized the single dharma-realm, various classes of beings give rise to various names, yet they do not destroy the dharma-realm.
Therefore, Śāriputra!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should don such armor as this: at that time, having realized the single Dharma-realm, I shall, by means of wisdom, explain the various names of sentient beings within their manifold realms; yet, through these manifold great wisdoms, one does not destroy the Dharma-realm, nor does the Dharma-realm become dual, nor can any increase or decrease in the Dharma-realm be known.

Śāriputra! Seeing this meaning, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate such a practice of the Dharma: although as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River have entered parinirvāṇa, no increase or decrease can be known in the dharma-dhātu;

likewise, all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, currently present in the worlds of the ten directions who possess unimpeded wisdom, and all the śrāvakas who possess limited wisdom—no increase or decrease can be known in the dharma-dhātu.
The realm of empty space is coextensive with the ultimate dharma-realm; know it thus: the dharma-realm is the ultimate, and one should likewise know that the Buddha-dharmas are coextensive with it.
Therefore, Śāriputra!
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should contemplate this profound Dharma with wisdom and realize the dharma of non-self. Śāriputra!
For example, just as there is nothing comparable to the realm of empty space, so it is, Śāriputra!"
The dharma-realm likewise has nothing with which it can be compared.
Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate this profound dharma with wisdom. Śāriputra!
For example, Śāriputra, it is as if someone were to take drops of water from the great ocean; they are all of one single taste, namely the taste of salt.
In this same way, Śāriputra, from the single Dharma-realm, śrāvakas are born.
Why is this? Because the dharma-realm is one and not two.
Therefore, Śāriputra!

Within this profound dharma, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should discern its deep points through wisdom; within this dharma, they should practice in accordance with the Prajñāpāramitā. It is not by means of extensive explanations or parables elsewhere that one should contemplate, observe, seek, and harmonize with the dharma of non-self; rather, one should give rise to the mind of aspiration, exert diligence, perform the work, and apply effort.
Sons of good family and daughters of good family, within this profound Dharma, you should perceive and awaken to the dharma of non-self through wisdom.

Śāriputra, it is as if there were fish in the great ocean whose bodies are one hundred yojanas long, even up to those whose bodies are seven hundred yojanas long. Although the bodies of those fish may grow to seven hundred yojanas, no increase or decrease can be seen in the great ocean; likewise, when those fish with bodies seven hundred yojanas long die, no increase or decrease can be seen in the great ocean.
Thus, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way:

although there may be as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River who have entered parinirvāṇa, no increase or decrease in the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) can be perceived;
furthermore, although there may be immeasurable śrāvakas who enter parinirvāṇa, no increase or decrease in the dharma-realm can be perceived.
Although this has but a single flavor, namely the flavor of liberation, the śrāvakas are unable to give rise to this wisdom in the same way as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
“Śāriputra! For example, when the various jewels of a wheel-turning monarch appear, those jewels do not arise elsewhere; they are produced solely within the royal palace.”
Why is this? Because that wheel-turning king, having performed the karma of a wheel-turning king in the past, produced all manner of jewels solely within his palace by virtue of that performed karma.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Pure Mind, having purified his mind and resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, if he wishes to give to others, whatever they desire shall be produced for them.
Why is this? Because of their pure and wholesome minds from previous lives.
