The Mahāsannipāta-sūtra-rāja-parikathā, Scroll II, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty. “Śāriputra!
It is as if there were a person who, having entered a treasure-mine—a place from which jewels are extracted—asked those who had entered before him:”
He said:
"O Noble Sir!
What are these various jewels like? What are their characteristics?"
The one who had entered first replied to that person, saying:
"O man! You are deluded;
how can you say you have entered the nature of jewels?"
"Having seen these various jewels, he further asks about them.
In this way, Śāriputra, if sons of good family or daughters of good family were to ask such a question: "What is the Dharma-realm like?"
"What are the characteristics of the dharma-realm? Śāriputra!
At that time, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should don such armor as this: 'I shall now reveal this dharma-realm to sentient beings and teach it so that they may abide within it.'"
Śāriputra! That which is called the "nature of jewels" is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Those who enter the nature of jewels yet inquire after the jewels are the foolish, ordinary worldlings.
Regarding those who have first entered the nature of the jewel, namely the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha:
Śāriputra, it is as if the great ocean does not form this thought:
"I shall produce various mani-jewels of measurable value, or I shall produce various mani-jewels of immeasurable value.
In this same way, Śāriputra,
the dharma-realm does not form such a thought:
"There may be those who know that I have emerged with limited knowledge, or those who have emerged with limitless knowledge. Śāriputra!

It is simply by following what is known within the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmadhātu) that one attains limited knowledge; and again, by following what is known within the fixed nature of phenomena, one attains limitless knowledge.
“Śāriputra! It is like this:
for example, before a day has ended, one knows how many kṣaṇas, how many lava-s, how many ghaṭī-s, and how many muhūrta-s there have been, knowing exactly how much of the day remains.”
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
[The truths of] suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path have not yet been fully brought forth. Therefore, Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, you should know that this is my teaching on the Bodhisattva Vehicle for those sons of good family and daughters of good family who have not yet reached bodhi. Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, it is just as when a mass of water falls upon the great earth; it does not cause the space to increase.

In the same way, Śāriputra, although as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River have already entered parinirvāṇa, the dharma-realm is seen neither to increase nor to decrease.
Though infinite assemblies of śrāvakas pass into parinirvāṇa, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is seen neither to increase nor to decrease.
Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should don such armor:

"The realm of sentient beings is seen neither to increase nor to decrease, and the dharma-realm is also seen neither to increase nor to decrease. We shall utter such a lion’s roar until we awaken to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! For example, it is impossible, as I have declared, that there could be a person who goes before the Dragon King of the Ocean and says:
"I wish to split a hair-tip into a hundred parts, and from one part of that hair, draw forth a single drop of water."
Then the Dragon King Sāgara said to that man: "O noble sir!
Even if you were to divide the tip of a hair into a hundred parts and draw out a single drop of water with one part of that hair, I would not abandon the great ocean."
"Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Within the boundless realm of sentient beings, he teaches and exerts power to bring about joy and great joy, saying to them:
'We are not capable of setting forth toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"Moreover, Śāriputra, I do not make any distinctions regarding the Dharma.
Śāriputra, it is like this:
during the hot season of late spring or summer, suppose someone goes to the great river Gaṅgā wishing to drink its water, and another person obstructs them, refusing to let them drink."
Śāriputra, what do you think? Would that person,
by creating an obstruction within that masterless mass of great water, be able to succeed in doing so?
He replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:

"Śāriputra, it is thus: within the dharma-realm that is without grasping and within the state of all buddha-dharmas that is without grasping, there are sons and daughters of good family who have resolved upon the Great Vehicle and possess faith, understanding, and longing; yet there are sentient beings who speak of the faults of the Great Vehicle, seeking to cause them to turn away from it and to sever their practice."
"Śāriputra, what do you think?
Would that person be acting in accordance with the Dharma?
He replied:
"No, Blessed One! No."
"Sugata! The Buddha said,
"Therefore, Śāriputra!"

When sons of good family and daughters of good family have heard this teaching, they should swiftly resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and generate the desire, diligence, and appropriate application of effort.
Sons of good family and daughters of good family, within this profound Dharma, you should contemplate with wisdom and realize the dharma of non-self. Śāriputra!
For example, there may be portions of land within this great earth that are of no use to the people of Jambudvīpa.
What are those? They are so-called pits, ravines, precipices, thorns, and high, steep, desolate places.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Within the realm of sentient beings, there are certain beings who are of no use to other sentient beings.
Who are they? They are those who have set out upon the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; such individuals are of no use to other sentient beings.
Śāriputra! It is like a portion of the great earth that people of Jambudvīpa find useful. What is it?
That is to say, they possess gardens, groves, and lotus ponds, and wherever there are sources of gold and silver, the people of Jambudvīpa are able to enjoy them.
In this same way, Śāriputra!
Within the realm of sentient beings, there are those who are of service to other sentient beings, yet they are few.
Who are they? They are those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for they act as a refuge for all sentient beings by ultimately bringing them happiness.
“Śāriputra! For example, although there are priceless maṇi jewels within the great ocean, the people of Jambudvīpa are unable to make use of them.
In the same way, Śāriputra!”

Although the Arhats and Śrāvakas possess boundless roots of goodness—namely, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—these qualities are of no use to sentient beings.

Just as all the roots of goodness—morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—possessed by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are for the enjoyment of all sentient beings.
Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should don such armor:
"If my roots of goodness do not result in the enjoyment of all sentient beings and ultimately bring them happiness, they are not my roots of goodness."
Śāriputra! For example, although the fruit of the nyagrodha tree is small in form, when it grows, it extends over and covers a vast area.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

When the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva first produce the thought of enlightenment arise and endure for a long time, one should know that they surpass all other roots of goodness and abide in the most supreme state.
Therefore, Śāriputra,

when sons of good family or daughters of good family who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle possess even small roots of goodness, they must not be treated with contempt, nor should it be said that these do not increase.
Why is this? Śāriputra, you should know that when the roots of goodness of one who has set out in the Mahāyāna increase, they become immeasurable and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya). Śāriputra!

For example, suppose there is a person who is immensely wealthy, possessing abundant riches and many articles of enjoyment, including numerous shells, gems, coral, gold, silver, and so forth—such as the son of a great kṣatriya family, the son of a great brāhmaṇa family, or the son of a great householder family. When such individuals go out into the streets and markets, whoever wishes to see them may do so; whoever wishes to approach them may do so; and whoever wishes to question them may do so.

At that time, all the various precious great maṇi jewels were worth many hundreds of thousands; those who wished to see them could see them, those who wished to approach them could approach them, and those who wished to inquire about them could inquire. Why was this?
They possess great minds regarding this buying and selling. Thus, Śāriputra,
within this Great Vehicle of all the Buddha-dharmas, a bodhisattva mahāsattva may ask whatever they wish to ask and speak whatever they wish to speak.
Why is this? Because they possess great faith;
thus their discourse is uninterrupted: those who wish to arrive do so, those who wish to inquire do so, those who wish to look do so, and those who wish to speak do so.
“Śāriputra! For example, all great maṇi jewels are of such great value that they are worth many hundreds of thousands.
Śāriputra!”
"What do you think?
Could that precious mani-jewel possibly coexist with crystal?
He replied:
"No, Blessed One! No."
Sugata! For what reason?
World-Honored One!
"That maṇi jewel dwells together with other maṇi jewels; it does not associate with crystal and the like, nor can they serve as its analogies.
The Buddha said, "So it is, Śāriputra!"

Noble sons and noble daughters of the Bodhisattva vehicle should dwell together, act together, and travel together with those beings who have set out in the Mahāyāna; they should draw near to them, follow their instructions, attend to them, perform good deeds for them, and cultivate many practices together. Within that context, they should awaken them and cause them to remember [the teachings], and by means of this, they should accordingly train themselves.
Śāriputra! It is as if there were a person who wished to learn archery; he should recollect and attend upon an archery master. Why is that?

While he trains in this place, the teacher must repeatedly prompt him to recall the instructions and offer encouragement, saying: "The bow is grasped thus; the fist is formed thus; the bow is held thus; the arrow is released thus. Because the archery teacher prompts him to recall and encourages him, he follows the training and shall achieve success.
In this way, Śāriputra!
Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who have set out in the Great Vehicle should draw near to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and follow him with offerings;
[they should do so] toward those who have set out in the Great Vehicle.
Noble sons and noble daughters should dwell together, act together, travel together, and attend to one another with mindfulness.
Those who have set out in the Great Vehicle—having approached, followed, and made offerings to them—should be awakened and reminded therein;
furthermore, they should be comforted and consoled, so that they may be awakened and reminded therein.
And when offering consolation and encouragement, they should train accordingly:
"This is the dāna-pāramitā; this is the śīla-pāramitā; this is the kṣānti-pāramitā;
this is the vīrya-pāramitā; this is the dhyāna-pāramitā; this is the prajñā-pāramitā."
This is the perfection of skillful means; one should train in this way.
Regarding all roots of goodness pertaining to universal knowledge, one should cause them to be awakened and remembered within that interval, and further provide consolation;
thus, by training accordingly, one shall achieve accomplishment.

“Śāriputra! For example, wherever a wheel-turning monarch travels within Jambudvīpa, the people of Jambudvīpa are not startled, nor terrified, nor harmed, nor injured; they generously bestow gold and silver, establish themselves in the ten paths of wholesome action, and practice in this manner.”
When that wheel-turning king travels, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of sentient beings weep with sorrow, remembering the virtues of the wheel-turning king.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas travel or wander through various Buddha-fields, they should train in the supreme virtues of the Buddhas; wherever they go, they should act in accordance with the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). In the places where they travel, they should ensure that sentient beings are not startled, terrified, harmed, or injured. Abounding in gold and silver, they should cause sentient beings to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action (daśakuśalakarmapatha) and cause them to give rise to these ten wholesome paths in ever-increasing measure. They should proceed in this manner until reaching the stage of outflowlessness (anāsrava-bhūmi). They should perform all their activities in this way, thinking: "These people should learn and keep in mind that this is the practice of my good friend—the one who gathers them into all wholesome dharmas, who provides strength, who brings awakening, who explains the profound points, and who gathers us in; this is the place where he travels."
Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in such supreme and exalted virtues. Śāriputra!

For example, wherever that wheel-turning monarch travels and proceeds, at that time many hundreds of thousands of koṭis, nayutas, and immeasurable sentient beings rejoice and desire his arrival. Why is this?
He teaches all sentient beings with wholesome dharmas; he gathers all sentient beings through wholesome dharmas.
Thus, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should don such armor:

"In whatever place I go, and in whatever successive realms I travel, throughout various directions and Buddha-fields, at that time there will be many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings who, filled with joy, will desire my coming."
Why is this? Because they shall teach the wholesome dharmas to all sentient beings, and furthermore, they shall gather in sentient beings through various skillful means. Śāriputra!
For example, Śāriputra, suppose there were a great maṇi jewel worth many hundreds of thousands; when one seeks it, from where would it be obtained?
It would be obtained at the place where it is sold.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, according to their skillful means, perceive those sentient beings who are capable of becoming vessels; they employ skillful means in various places to instruct them in roots of goodness. Subsequently, having sought out various kinds of skillful means, they teach sentient beings to harmonize with the wholesome dharmas and exhort them toward the mind of bodhi.

Śāriputra! It is, for example, as when the sons of various kings or the sons of royal ministers gather together and sit, deliberating thus: "In this way we shall take the royal throne; we shall establish the royal laws; we shall uphold the royal throne; and we shall proclaim the royal edicts."
In this way, Śāriputra,
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fervently cultivate all roots of goodness; they serve many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of buddhas and plant various roots of goodness,
skillfully cultivating loving-kindness and always being able to maintain universal mindfulness.
They practice the bodhicitta of great compassion and joy; they practice equanimity by recollecting the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Such persons of great faith—who wish to let out the lion’s roar, who wish to pour down the rain of Dharma, who wish to beat the drum of Dharma, who wish to blow the conch of Dharma, who wish to raise the banner of Dharma, and who wish to establish the Dharma... [are those who]... practice equanimity by recollecting the site of enlightenment.

Those such as these, being of great faith, desire to let out the lion’s roar, desire to pour down the rain of Dharma, desire to beat the drum of Dharma, desire to blow the conch of Dharma, desire to raise the banner of Dharma, and desire to establish the Dharma.
The boat is for those who wish to ferry across all sentient beings fallen into the four currents; for those who wish to don the armor for immeasurable eons;
for those who wish to don the firm armor of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity;
for those who wish to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; for those who wish to subdue Māra and his retinue; and for those who wish to don the inconceivable armor.

Those who wish to don the incomparable armor, those who wish to don the most excellent and supreme armor among all the three realms—such sons of noble family as these gathered together in one place and deliberated thus:
"We should gather all sentient beings within those untainted roots of goodness. I...
We should cause all sentient beings to dedicate themselves toward the realm of nirvāṇa;
we should bring rest to all sentient beings within the unconditioned realm of nirvāṇa.
“Śāriputra! For example, when the sons of various kings or the sons of royal ministers are gathered and seated together, other low-born persons may not go to that place.”
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gather and sit together, other beings who possess only a small portion of wisdom cannot perceive or demonstrate such a realm as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest.

Śāriputra! For example, in the great ocean there are sentient beings whose bodies are as large as a louse, and there are sentient beings whose bodies are a hundred yojanas in size, and there are even sentient beings whose bodies reach seven hundred yojanas.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Does that great ocean not contain those sentient beings with small bodies, as well as those sentient beings with large bodies?
He replied, “No, Blessed One.”
"No, Sugata! It is not that the great ocean cannot contain it."
World-Honored One!
It is due to the karma they have created that those beings are born with small bodies;
it is due to the karma they have created that those beings are born with large bodies.
The Buddha said:
"It is so, Śāriputra!

Because of the power of their vows, the śrāvakas possess little wisdom; however, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, incomparable, boundless, and ineffable wisdom."

Why is this? Because in the past, while practicing the bodhisattva path, he formed immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, incomparable, boundless, and ineffable vows; by accomplishing those karmas, he has reached the supreme merit of unimpeded knowledge.
Śāriputra! It is as if there were various sentient beings in the great ocean who, not being in proximity to or united with a maṇi jewel, do not even know its name, let alone make use of it.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

There are sons of good family who are born into this Dharma and Vinaya and who traverse that ocean of Dharma to its full extent; yet even the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not know the names of those samādhis, let alone those who wish to practice while fully possessing all samādhis.
Because he is fully possessed of these samādhis, he is called the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“Śāriputra! Just as when a master archer employs his manual skill and technique, the place where he releases an arrow is never missed;
so it is, Śāriputra!”

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, through skillful means, gather [beings] with skillful means and are fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). When such beings resolve their minds, it shall immediately not be in vain; there is nothing they do not gather, and nothing they do not dedicate toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
That bodhicitta does not enter into desire, hatred, or delusion; it is not defiled by desire, not repelled by hatred, and not bewildered by delusion.

When one generates that bodhicitta, it does not enter into form, nor even into consciousness; it does not enter into the self, nor even into sensation; it is not the realm of the eye, nor the realm of forms; it does not enter the realm of eye-consciousness, nor even the realm of the mind, nor the realm of phenomena; it does not enter the realm of mind-consciousness.

If one gives rise to the bodhicitta, one is immediately free from desire, hatred, and delusion; if there is no desire, hatred, or delusion, then there is great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; if there is great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, then there is nothing to be apprehended; if there is nothing to be apprehended, then there is neither arising nor ceasing; if there is neither arising nor ceasing, then there is neither annihilation nor permanence; if there is neither annihilation nor permanence, this is called giving rise to the bodhicitta. It is the ultimate limit of the realm of space and the ultimate consummation of the dharma-realm; it is the union of the karma of the realm of space with the wisdom of skillful means—this is called giving rise to the bodhicitta.
“Śāriputra! For example, when a jewel tree grows and matures, it is not devoid of the functional capacity for various jewels.
In the same way, Śāriputra!”
The bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, collectively encompassing great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity.
Śāriputra!
For this reason, you should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is like a jewel tree.

Śāriputra! Suppose all the trees, grasses, branches, and leaves in this trichiliocosm were made into lamp wicks; suppose all the Sumeru Kings, Cakravāḍa Mountains, Mahācakravāḍa Kings, Mucilinda Mountains, Mahāmucilinda Kings, as well as all other Black Mountains and rocky mountains in this trichiliocosm were made into lamp vessels; and suppose all the springs, ponds, lakes, rivers, small streams, great rivers, and great oceans in this trichiliocosm were filled with oil. If sons or daughters of good family belonging to the Śrāvaka-yāna or Pratyekabuddha-yāna were to light those lamps before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Would those sons of good family or daughters of good family, by reason of that cause and condition, have much merit?
He replied, “Very many, Blessed One!”
"Very many, Great Virtuous Sugata!
the Buddha said.
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has set out in the Great Vehicle were to offer even a single lamp, by reason of that cause and condition, which would have the greater merit?”
When he had spoken thus, Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!

One who has set out in the Great Vehicle generates even greater merit by offering a single lamp than one who belongs to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the pratyekabuddhas by offering boundless, incalculable, and immeasurable lamps.”
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, excellent, excellent!"
Śāriputra! It is so, it is so, just as you have said. Why is that?
If the *dānapāramitā* of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the *dānapāramitā* of all sentient beings,
then through the *dānapāramitā* of those bodhisattvas, all those sentient beings shall obtain the various articles of enjoyment, such as food, drink, clothing, ornaments, and vehicles.

If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), those sentient beings will immediately obtain various articles for enjoyment such as the wealth, grain, and storehouses of householders, as well as articles for enjoyment such as fields, houses, gardens, groves, palaces, cities, towns, villages, kingdoms, and royal capitals.
Śāriputra! To speak briefly, there are the bodhisattvas' śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, and prajñā.
Those sentient beings who have violated their śīla, up to and including those who lack wisdom, shall thereby attain wisdom.

Why is this? One should view that initial generation of the mind as being like sowing seeds; one’s subsequent practice is like the growth of those seeds; the stage of non-retrogression is like the formation of branches and leaves; the stage of being destined for birth in the next life is like the emergence of flowers; and the stage of the Tathāgata is like the ripening of fruit. According to the desires of sentient beings, the fruit thus gathers; one should view the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata in this same way.

Śāriputra! For this reason, you should know that it is through the initial aspiration for awakening that the Tathāgata is born; it is through the Tathāgata that all the requisites of happiness for sentient beings arise, and it is also through the Tathāgata that the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas arise.
Śāriputra!
For this reason, all roots of goodness possessed by sons of good family and daughters of good family should be dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Śāriputra! For example, when the lunar disk rises, all the springs, ponds, lakes, pools, rivers, small streams, and great rivers in this Jambudvīpa all behold the lunar disk there; yet that Moon Devaputra does not move from his own palace, and that lunar disk does not approach any single location, yet the reflection of the lunar disk appears in all places.”
In this way, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the tenth stage manifests his own body in many buddha-fields— indeed, in as many as hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of buddha-fields— in all places such as villages, cities, market towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals within those buddha-fields.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests his own person, appearing in some places as the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). He may give away his head, hands, feet, eyes, or ears; he may give away his skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, or heart; he may give away his children, wife, concubines, houses, villages, towns, settlements, kingdoms, or royal capitals. Or he may manifest a great assembly for the blameless dharma-sacrifice, providing food to those who need food and drink to those who need drink, and so on, up to providing vehicles, clothing, garlands, incense, ointments, seats, couches, pillows, and lamps. When he manifests such acts of relinquishment, it is for the sake of gathering in sentient beings who are stingy and miserly, and even for the sake of abandoning the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).

In some places, he manifests the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), which is unimpaired, unpierced, unblemished, and unmixed—just as a yak protects its tail—for the sake of gathering in sentient beings who have broken their precepts, and even to lead them to abide in the three gates of liberation.

In some places, he manifests the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); even when his hands and feet are severed or his eyes are gouged out, he remains free from anger. This is for the sake of gathering in those sentient beings who are arrogant and poisoned by hatred, as well as those who are addicted to wealth and status, and ultimately to lead them to abide in the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In some places, he manifests the *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of vigor) in order to incite diligent effort in indolent sentient beings; to cause them to weary of their own pleasures and lead all sentient beings to abide in true happiness; to gather in those sentient beings who are indolent or possess only slight vigor and establish them in vigor; and even to lead them to abide in the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

In some places, he manifests the perfection of dhyāna, sporting in the liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis of dhyāna; this is for the sake of gathering in those sentient beings whose mindfulness is lost, who lack correct awareness, who lack samādhi, and whose minds are distracted, even unto leading them to abide in the vajra-samādhi.

In some places, he manifests the *prajñāpāramitā*, because he teaches the profound Buddha-dharma that is difficult to realize; he teaches according to the conduct of sentient beings regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), and what is the ground and what is not the ground (*bhūmibhūmi*).
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the tenth stage is skillfully endowed with the means of integration and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). He is able to act exactly as he desires; according to how sentient beings have faith in the various perfections, he manifests those perfections for them; according to how sentient beings have faith in form (rūpa), he manifests form for them; and according to their faith in the fundamental nature of phenomena (dharmatā), he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, so that those beings shall attain non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

“Śāriputra! It is like a tree that can grant all desires; if there are sentient beings who come to its side desiring various jewels, it causes those beings to have their wishes fulfilled—whether they be food, clothing, or necklaces.”
Whatever treasures those sentient beings require—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, agate, and musaragalva—if there is anything they desire, those treasures immediately appear.

For that tree which fulfills all the desires of sentient beings, even if it is cut, split, or hewn, no place of cutting, splitting, or damage can be seen; rather, it grows ever more and produces various kinds of jewels.
In this way, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the tenth stage manifests the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) in some places,
and manifests the perfections of ethical discipline (śīla), patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditation (dhyāna), and wisdom (prajñā) in other places.
The perfection of wisdom has skillful means as its foremost feature; in some places, it manifests birth among the gods of the Four Great Kings,
the Thirty-three Gods, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven,
and the various Māra-body heavens, up to the various Brahma-body heavens and the Brahmā-purohita Heaven.
The Brahmakāyika devas, the Brahmapurohita devas, the Mahābrahmā devas, the Ābhāsvara devas,
the Parīttābhā devas, the Apramāṇābhā devas, the Śubha devas, the Parīttaśubha devas, the Apramāṇaśubha devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, the Vṛhatphala devas, the Parīttaśubha devas,
the Apramāṇaśubha devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, the Bṛhatphala devas, and the Atapa devas.
In the Sudṛśa Heaven and the Sudarśana Heaven, and even up to being born in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, he manifests his own body and preaches the Dharma.

In some places, he manifests as beings with perception and without perception, up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; in other places, he manifests in this Jambudvīpa as the body of a Wheel-Turning King to preach the Dharma for sentient beings.

In some places he manifests the physical form of a wheel-turning monarch possessing one-quarter of the [four] divisions; in some places he manifests the physical form of a powerful wheel-turning monarch.

In some places he manifests the forms of kṣatriyas, householders, great ministers, royal officials, young boys and girls, women and men, śramaṇas, brahmins, nirgranthas, brahmans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, and even those who dwell in cities.
In some places he manifests the physical forms of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

in other places he manifests descending from Tuṣita Heaven, or entering the mother’s womb, or being born, or being received by Brahmā and Śakra, or taking seven steps, or uttering words from his mouth:
"I am the most honored and supreme in the world; I shall bring an end to birth and death."

"Sometimes he goes to a schoolhouse, or enters a deva temple, or stays within a palace, or remains beneath a Jambu tree; sometimes he leaves the household life, or arrives at a site of enlightenment, or subdues the hosts of Māra’s army, or realizes unsurpassed bodhi, or turns the wheel of Dharma, or preaches the Dharma for the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, or manifests nirvāṇa; sometimes his entire body remains, or it is like a mustard seed; sometimes he causes the True Dharma to blaze forth, or he manifests the extinction of the Dharma."

“Śāriputra! To speak briefly, those who preach the Dharma according to the inclinations of sentient beings are the manifestations of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas themselves, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity.”

Just as all sentient beings have faith in the fundamental nature of all phenomena, so too do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas expound the fundamental nature of phenomena for the sake of all sentient beings, causing those sentient beings to attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra!
It is as if a magician, or a magician’s apprentice, were to stand at a great crossroads and display various illusions, namely: elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Can the places from which and to which those fourfold armies come and go be known within the worlds of the ten directions?
He replied, “No, Blessed One.”
"No, Sugata! The coming and going of that illusion cannot be known, yet that illusion is not without a cause."
The Buddha said:
"It is so, Śāriputra!

Whether that Buddha’s wisdom comes or goes, it cannot be known even within the worlds of the ten directions. Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is fully endowed with this wisdom, he knows, exactly as they are, all the mental activities of all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Yet that wisdom is not without cause; that wisdom is supreme, and it should be viewed in this way."
Śāriputra! Just as when someone is seized by the throat, all the sense faculties are thereby seized;
so it is, Śāriputra!

If sons or daughters of good family enter into the Buddha-dharmas with a mind of universal knowledge and a mind of awakening, they invite all sentient beings, gather in all sentient beings, and sustain all sentient beings.
Śāriputra!
For example, suppose there were a person with a lifespan of a hundred years who brought a single drop of water and offered it to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I entrust this single drop of water to you; I pray that you will hold it and not let it mingle with other waters.
Having accepted it, the Tathāgata cast it into the great river Gaṅgā, and once cast, that single drop of water flowed toward the great ocean.
Then, when those people who lived for a hundred years had passed that year and returned, they spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
Give me that single drop of water which I previously entrusted to you, ensuring it was not mixed with any other water."

“Śāriputra! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses such wisdom—namely, inconceivable wisdom, incomparable wisdom, and wisdom that transcends the triple world. Having been endowed with this wisdom, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha emerges from the great ocean and returns that single drop of water previously entrusted to him, unmixed with any other water, to that person.”
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not teach the Dharma within only one buddha-field, nor within two, three, four, five, or even up to a thousand buddha-fields; rather, he teaches and transforms sentient beings through various skillful means.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha teaches the Dharma within immeasurable, incalculable, inexpressible, and infinite thousands of Buddha-fields, employing various skillful means to transform and guide sentient beings.

“Śāriputra! It is as if, during the height of the summer heat following spring, a man were traveling with a great multitude through a wilderness. While on the way, he sees from afar shimmering mirages moving, and he consoles that multitude, saying:
‘Come along; there is water to drink.’”

At that time, that person caused the great assembly to maintain their hope for water without interruption; they quickly emerged from the wilderness and found relief, remaining unhurt and uninjured, arriving safely and fearlessly at their own destination.

In this way, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, teaches the Dharma to the śrāvakas who wish to enter the fruit of arhatship. Just as an arhat applies himself with diligence and effort in accordance with what must be done, once he has performed those tasks, he attains their benefit.
Śāriputra! If one has faith in this Dharma, they have faith in the dustless Dharma;
if one has faith in the dustless Dharma, they have faith in the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
If one has faith in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, one is liberated in the dustless Dharma;
if one is liberated in the dustless Dharma, one is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
Śāriputra!

For example, when an Arhat who has exhausted all outflows recites while staying in a remote and perilous place such as an araṇya mountain, an echo arises there; at that time, another person who hears it immediately attains the fruit of Arhatship.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Who is it that has tamed that person?
He replied,
“World-Honored One,
he is an arhat.”
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra, what do you think?"
"How could that Arhat, whose outflows are exhausted, ever entertain such a thought as:
'When I recite [the teachings], will there be sentient beings who attain taming? He replied:
"No, Blessed One! No."
“Sugata! The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!”
What do you think?
Does that echo come from within, from without, or from both within and without?
Do not hold such a view.
If the words and speech uttered by sentient beings should be believed in this way, and if there is such a statement, they too follow me. Śāriputra!
It is as if a man or a woman, while in a dream, were to see the Tathāgata surrounded by a multitude of śrāvakas preaching the Dharma.
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Do the śrāvakas of the Tathāgata actually come?
He replied:
"No, Blessed One! No."
“Sugata! The Buddha said,
“So it is, Śāriputra!”

If a person currently sees me preaching the Dharma surrounded by my assembly of śrāvakas, they should believe it to be like a dream; such a person then directly beholds me, as well as the Dharma and the Saṃgha. Śāriputra!
For example, it is not that the great ocean lacks jewels such that one does not take them. Why is this?
Because in previous lives, one did not perform the karma of taking jewels; therefore, one does not recognize or take the black *maṇi* jewel.
If a person has previously performed the karma for a maṇi jewel, they will enter the island of jewels; having entered the island of jewels, they will take up the maṇi jewels.
In this same way, Śāriputra!
It is not that the dharma-realm does not exist, yet they do not awaken to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Śāriputra!

It is simply because in their previous lives they did not cultivate roots of goodness nor give rise to them within the sphere of the Buddhas; therefore, they have now entered the stage of the śrāvaka. They do not practice the domain of the Tathāgatas, nor do they possess the merits of a Tathāgata; they are not endowed with the powers, fearlessnesses, and unimpeded wisdom of a Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is endowed with the powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth, as well as unimpeded wisdom. Śāriputra!
For example, just as a man or a woman takes up a mirror and looks at their own face; seeing their own facial features, they immediately give rise to joy and exultation.
In the same way, Śāriputra, because unlearned ordinary persons do not understand that the nature of phenomena is like a reflection, they run about in saṃsāra, giving rise to craving and attachment.
Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should don such armor as this: "I shall now preach the Dharma for all sentient beings, so that they may come to know and sever the cycle of saṃsāra."
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should have faith that all phenomena are empty, void, and unsubstantial;
in this manner, they should practice. Śāriputra!

For example, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha manifests a magical creation, that creation is not born when it arises and does not perish when it ceases. Whether questioned or answering within the Buddha’s realm, these are not two separate things; for that which is manifested by the Tathāgata is not born when it arises and does not perish when it ceases.

Thus, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) awakens to the non-arising of all phenomena; having awakened, they do not apprehend a single phenomenon. Whether in the moment of arising, that which arises is a phenomenon that has no locus of arising; or in the moment of ceasing, that which ceases is likewise neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Why is this? Because, Śāriputra, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize that all dharmas are non-dual. Śāriputra!
For example, a mass of foam has no solidity; one should understand in accordance with the fact that it lacks solidity.
In this same way, Śāriputra!

All phenomena lack solidity; all phenomena are empty, and one should understand them in accordance with this. All phenomena are like the ocean, for their fundamental nature is without dual characteristics.
Śāriputra!
For example, a bubble of water arises from causes and conditions; it cannot arise through any single cause alone.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

Whatever sentient beings, due to improper mindfulness, desire to take up birth—all that is empty, void, and not solid; those sentient beings do not know reality as it truly is within the sphere of ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), nor do they see it, enter it, or awaken to it.
"For the sake of those sentient beings, I have in the past donned such armor as this: 'How may I cause those sentient beings to perceive the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
I shall explain to them the cycle of saṃsāra.'"
“Śāriputra! Just as when a bird travels through space there is no dharma that can obstruct it, so too, Śāriputra,

when sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle have faith in omniscience within the limit of non-obstruction, the limit of dustlessness, and the limit of non-duality regarding all dharmas— I say that these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle are certain to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Śāriputra! It is like a bhikṣu with supernormal powers who travels through space; although one sees him travel, one does not see his footprints.
In the same way, Śāriputra!
They may observe the conduct of a bodhisattva, yet they are unable to explain that Dharma or the point of dedication of those roots of goodness.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

The Dharma realized by me is ineffable; that Dharma cannot be accomplished by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans, except for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are preeminent in all worlds, endowed with supreme wisdom, and clad in the great armor.
Why is this? Śāriputra, all the worlds, including the devas and others, cannot equal that bodhisattva mahāsattva. Śāriputra!
Just as hands and feet are able to perform all manner of tasks, so too,
Śāriputra, should one view this fundamental teaching.
Śāriputra! Suppose there were a person who could point out five fingers with a single finger.
What do you think? Would that be a difficult feat to perform?
Śāriputra said:
"It is extremely difficult, Bhagavān!"
"It is extremely difficult, Sugata!
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! This teaching of mine is difficult, for it is like the dharma-realm which is equal to space. Having awakened to the dharma that is equal to space, to explain this difficulty to others—that, I say, is marvelous.”
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having awakened to the dharmas that are equal to space, are able to increase [their practice] without engaging in conceptual proliferation.
In this way, Śāriputra!

All the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is to awaken to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are all void, non-existent, empty, and not solid. Only when *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* has been manifested do those roots of goodness become non-deceptive, and one awakens to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should don such armor, thinking:

"I believe that all dharmas are not solid; if one does not enter this patience, one cannot accomplish the dharma of the eight types of persons, nor the dharma of a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, or an arhat, let alone awaken to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—except for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who possess supreme and perfect wisdom, being the most excellent within the three realms."
Śāriputra! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should draw near to virtuous friends, serving and making offerings to them.
Who are these virtuous friends?
This refers to instructing and teaching the practice of the six pāramitās.
If one teaches by other means, they are not a virtuous friend.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva speaks thus, teaches thus, and says, "In this way you should study the various pāramitās; in this way you should study the various bodhisattva-dharmas," then one should know that such a person is called a true virtuous friend of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Śāriputra! For example, suppose one were to cast a single drop of ghee into the great ocean;
what do you think? Is this much or not?
Śāriputra said: “No, Blessed One.”
"No, Sugata! Within that water,
it would still be but a single drop."
The Buddha said: "So it is,
so it is, Śāriputra!"

The morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are limited in their inclusion; they are unable to bring benefit to all sentient beings.
Śāriputra! It is as if a single drop of oil were thrown into a pool of flowers; it would then completely permeate them, yet one would not know the nature of that drop of oil.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

The morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as all their roots of goodness, are for the sake of sentient beings so that they may enjoy them until they reach ultimate nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! Suppose there were a man in the great ocean who, having split a single hair into a hundred parts, took up a single drop of water with it.
What do you think?
“Compared to the mass of water in the great ocean, which of these two is greater:
that single drop of water or the great ocean? Śāriputra replied, “World-Honored One!”
"Even if one were to take a hundred yojanas [of water], it would still be but a small amount; how much more so when that person takes a single drop of water from a hair split into a hundred parts?
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"
In this way, the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is like a single drop of water, whereas the knowledge and vision of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is like a vast accumulation of ocean water.
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are fully endowed with such knowledge and vision, they are able to bring all sentient beings to maturity, even leading them to the realm of nirvana without remainder.

When the Buddha spoke this Dharma-foundation praising the merits of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, and boundless sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, and boundless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas saw their roots of goodness blaze forth and increase as they were exhorted toward the fulfillment of practice; and immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, and boundless devas and humans became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, as well as the other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had taught, were all greatly rejoiced.
